# Normal-bundle convex order at an arbitrary finite-fiber local minimum

This note removes curvature and polyhedrality from the feasible normal
variations, and retains cap/body facet coincidences in their derivatives.
It is a necessary-condition theorem at an unrestricted local minimum,
not a proof of the OC depth constant. The resulting boundary transport
still has to be used in a genuine global argument.

UPDATE 2026-09-18: the numerical target gamma_d/h(P) on arbitrary finite
bases is exactly FALSE; see the unequal-three-site counterexample note.
For OC, apply these necessary conditions only together with the retained
arithmetic base information in `candidate 2086e4eaa4bce465`.
Its parity-budget reduction uses gamma_d/k(U) on a lattice-complete base.

## 1. Actual families and section support functions

Let d>=1 and let P be a finite set in its affine span E. Let positive
compact convex bodies K_p in R^d satisfy every anchored Minkowski
inclusion. Put C=conv union_p({p} times K_p), B=conv P. Then C has
interior relative to E times R^d, and its p-section is exactly K_p.
Only the specified fibers at P are measured, with mu=sum_p vol_d.

For z in B and a unit vector u in R^d let h_z(u) be the support of
the actual continuous section C_z. Explicitly,

    h_z(u)=max{sum_p alpha_p h_p(u):
        alpha_p>=0, sum alpha_p=1, sum alpha_p p=z}.    (1)

Indeed C_z is the convex hull of the corresponding Minkowski sums.
The finite linear program proves that h_z(u) is concave and continuous
piecewise affine in z, and continuous jointly in(z,u). One way to
check boundary continuity is to use its finitely many feasible bases:
on the common polyhedral subdivision their values are affine in z
with coefficients continuous in u; their finite slopes are uniformly
bounded for u on the compact sphere. They agree on adjoining cells.

These supports are uniformly bounded. Moreover all C_z contain an
interior ball of one common positive radius: choose such balls in the
finitely many K_p and take their Minkowski combinations in(1).

## 2. Normal-dependent convex potentials give actual variations

Choose finitely many functions of the form

    A(u,z,x)=a_0(u)+a(u) dot z+b(u) dot x,

with continuous coefficients on the unit sphere, and finitely many
continuous convex functions Phi_l(z,x), with continuous weights
psi_l(u)>=0. Smooth convex functions and finite maxima of affine
functions are sufficient in everything below. Let

    V(u,z,x)=A(u,z,x)+sum_l t_l psi_l(u)Phi_l(z,x),
    t_l>=0.

For epsilon>=0 define

    C_epsilon={ (z,x):z in B,
          u dot x+epsilon V(u,z,x)<=h_z(u)
                    for EVERY unit u }.             (2)

Every defining inequality is convex in(z,x): its left side is convex
and its right side is concave. Thus C_epsilon is convex. It is closed
by joint continuity and the compact normal parameter. Every measured
fiber remains positive for small epsilon, since a fixed smaller
interior ball has a uniform initial support margin and V is bounded
on a fixed compact set around C.

The bodies are uniformly bounded for small epsilon. Each finite convex
Phi_l has an affine minorant, so V(u,z,x)>=-L(1+|x|) for z in compact B,
with one finite L independent of u. Testing u=x/|x| in(2) gives
(1-epsilon L)|x|<=H+epsilon L, where H uniformly bounds the supports.
This proves boundedness when epsilon L<1. Hence C_epsilon is an actual
convex body with positive measured fibers. Its sections are defined
EXACTLY by(2); no later compatibility repair is used.

The coefficients of A are signed and arbitrary. Thus every finite
collection of these affine directions is available with both signs.
The convex-potential terms have nonnegative coefficients. Finite sums
of all these directions are realized simultaneously by the SAME
construction(2), proving feasibility of the full parameter cone.

For a lattice-convex P, restricting the projection to B retains exactly
that integer base set. The finite-base formulation itself does not
silently count unlisted integer points.

## 3. First variations on arbitrary convex fiber boundaries

For surface-almost every x in boundary K_p, its outer unit normal n_p(x)
is unique. This is the ordinary convex-boundary regularity statement:
finitely many Lipschitz graph charts and Rademacher's theorem prove it.
Define the finite normal-bundle measure eta by

    int f deta=sum_p int_(boundary K_p)
                         f(n_p(x),p,x)dH_(d-1)(x).    (3)

For d=1 this means the two endpoints, with their two normals and H_0.
For d>=2 the exceptional nonregular points have zero surface measure.
Use the compact set of all supporting triples(u,p,x) as its containing
space; eta is supported on the unique-normal triples up to a null set.

The outward normal velocity under(2) is

    r(u,p,x)=-V(u,p,x),

and its exact mass derivative is

    M'(0+)=int r deta.                                (4)

Here is a direct justification, including nonsmooth bodies. Fix an
interior point c of K_p, an included ball of radius r_0, and an outer
radius R_0. Write its radial boundary as x=c+rho(omega)omega. Uniform
bounds on V in the bounded variation region sandwich K_p(epsilon)
between the inner and outer parallel bodies at distance O(epsilon).
These in turn are between homotheties about c of ratios1+O(epsilon)
and1-O(epsilon), because r_0 B is included in K_p-c. Thus the new
radial functions satisfy |rho_epsilon-rho|<=C epsilon uniformly.

At a regular radial endpoint, let u_0 be its unique support normal.
Any active normal u_epsilon at the new endpoint tends to u_0: a
different limit would support the original endpoint as well. Also
u_0 dot omega>=r_0/R_0>0. Testing the new endpoint in the inequality
for u_0 gives an upper limit for (rho_epsilon-rho)/epsilon of
-V(u_0,p,x)/(u_0 dot omega). The active u_epsilon equation, together
with its nonnegative original slack, gives the matching lower limit.
Therefore this is the exact radial derivative.

Radial parametrization and its inverse are Lipschitz for a convex
body containing a ball, so the nonregular endpoints have a null set
of directions. Differentiate |K_p(epsilon)|=(1/d)int rho_epsilon^d
by dominated convergence using the uniform O(epsilon) bound. The
radial surface Jacobian is rho^(d-1)/(u_0 dot omega); this proves(4).
For d=1 the same calculation is simply the change of its two endpoints.

For a fixed nonvertical cap H whose boundary does not contain a
positive-area body facet, the same argument gives

    (mu_epsilon(H))'(0+)=int r 1_H deta.               (5)

The cap indicator stabilizes at every boundary point except its
surface-null intersection with the cap plane. Uniform bounds justify
dominated convergence. Formula(5) is NOT used at a coincident facet;
the exact branch formulas below replace it there.

## 4. Moving caps and consistent facet allocations

Normalize each selected cap as

    H_j={a_j dot z+v_j dot x>=b_j}, |v_j|=1.

An affine cap-parameter velocity gives its relative margin velocity

    ell_j(z,x)=delta a_j dot z+delta v_j dot x-delta b_j.

On a proper fiber section the cap derivative contains the ordinary
coarea term int ell_j dH_(d-1). On the body boundary strictly inside
H_j it contains r; strictly outside it contains zero. At a coincident
supporting facet F the two possible branches are exactly

    min(r,ell_j),              if K_p is inside H_j,
    max(r+ell_j,0),            if K_p is outside H_j.  (6)

To see this, use outward normal coordinate tau at F. In the inside
case the moving body is tau<=epsilon r and the cap is
tau<=epsilon ell_j. In the outside case they are tau<=epsilon r
and tau>=-epsilon ell_j. Their signed thicknesses give(6).
Integrating on F is valid up to its null boundary. The remaining
intersection neighborhoods contribute o(epsilon): outside coincident
facets the surface measure within a shrinking cap-plane neighborhood
tends to zero, while displacement remains O(epsilon).

Represent an inside branch by alpha r+sigma ell_j with
alpha,sigma>=0 and alpha+sigma=1; represent an outside branch by
alpha r+sigma ell_j with alpha=sigma in[0,1]. The same two allocations
are used in the body and cap terms. On strict body interior cap traces
alpha=1, on strict exterior traces alpha=0. Let zeta_j be the effective
section measure: full ordinary measure on proper sections, sigma
times facet measure on coincidences, and zero on strictly full/empty
fibers. The candidate cap gradients are

    g_j=int alpha_j r deta+int ell_j dzeta_j.         (7)

All allowed measurable allocations give a compact convex set of
gradients on any fixed finite parameter space. This follows because
the densities lie in[0,1] on finitely many compact finite-measure
facets and only finitely many continuous moments are used. The actual
one-sided cap derivative is at most the supremum of(7): an endpoint
allocation realizes each min or max in(6). This upper bound is all
the separation argument needs.

There is a stronger quantifier. On each INSIDE coincidence one may
prescribe any Borel alpha in[0,1] in advance and fix sigma=1-alpha,
because min(r,ell)<=alpha r+(1-alpha)ell for every such choice. Let
only the outside allocations vary in the gradient sets. Every proof
below still applies to those smaller compact convex sets. Thus the
resulting certificate exists for EVERY prescribed system of inside
allocations, as well as for every selected critical cover. It may
depend on that system. The exact local cap condition and this
strengthening are proved separately in
`candidate 9c6d3cb586898f7e`.

Every selected critical cap through an interior anchor has a proper
section of positive area, and a positive-area body boundary patch
strictly inside it. Thus under common erosion r=-1 with all cap
parameters fixed, EVERY candidate gradient g_j is bounded above by
-c_j for one c_j>0. Coincident allocations cannot cancel this strict
negative contribution.

## 5. Selected circuit covers and normalized robust separation

Assume the family is an unrestricted local minimum of maximum
normalized depth beta>0. Put Q=beta M. Choose any finite collection
of critical positive circuit groups covering all deepest bases, and
keep fixed slack circuit covers at the remaining bases. The critical
caps all have mass Q. Their weights rho_ij>0 satisfy
sum_j rho_ij v_ij=0. Each group has specified base assignments with
covering margins sum_j rho_ij(a_ij dot p-b_ij)>=0.

Cap variations retain sum_j rho_ij delta v_ij=0. At each assigned
base where the original covering margin is zero, require its first
margin change to be nonnegative. Originally strict covering margins
stay positive for sufficiently small parameters. Since the cap
motions are affine, these constraints preserve the actual whole-fiber
closed cover. Together with nonnegative convex-potential coefficients
they define a closed finite-dimensional polyhedral cone D. All affine
body directions are free.

Write L_0=int r deta for the objective derivative and G_j for the
compact cap-gradient sets(7). One must have

    L_0 in cone(union_j G_j)+D^polar,
    D^polar={ell:ell(delta)<=0 for all delta in D}.   (8)

For completeness, this cone is closed. Pair a convergent sequence in
it with common erosion. Its uniformly negative pairing with all G_j
bounds the total nonnegative cap coefficient, since every polar term
also has nonpositive pairing with erosion. Compactness of the G_j
then gives a convergent cap part; the remaining polar part converges
in its closed cone. If(8) failed, strict separation would give a
direction delta in D with L_0(delta)>0 and sup_(g in G_j)g(delta)<=0
for every j. Adding a small positive erosion keeps the former positive
and makes every latter bound strictly negative. The actual finite
variation would increase total mass and place all critical cap masses
strictly below the old Q; slack caps and all assigned covers persist.
Its maximum normalized depth would be strictly below beta, a
contradiction. This proves(8).

Thus for consistent chosen allocations there are lambda_j>=0 and
ell in D^polar with L_0=sum_j lambda_j g_j+ell. There is no abnormal
zero objective multiplier: the objective itself is the element in(8).

Include signed joint continuous homothety among the finite directions:
r(u,p,x)=u dot x, delta v_j=0, delta a_j=a_j, delta b_j=b_j.
It is allowed by(2), to first order, and preserves every active cover.
Both signs belong to D. Every allocation in(7) has homothety value
dQ: on a proper section ell_j=-v_j dot x, while at a coincident
facet the inside branch has r=ell_j and the outside branch has
r+ell_j=0. The divergence theorem gives L_0=dM. The polar term is
zero on this signed direction. Consequently

    sum_j lambda_j=1/beta.                            (9)

## 6. One certificate for all normal-localized tests

The multipliers and weighted allocations can be chosen to handle
ALL the normal-localized tests simultaneously. Here are the compactness
details. Always include erosion and the two homotheties. Equation(9)
places lambda in a fixed compact simplex. On each coincident facet
store the WEIGHTED allocation measures lambda_j alpha_j and
lambda_j sigma_j, rather than their quotients. They are dominated
by lambda_j times the fixed facet measure. The inside sum and outside
equality relations are linear and weakly closed. Their compact
measure spaces and the fixed proper-section parts therefore give
one compact space of candidate certificates, independent of the
number of body tests.

For any finite list of tests, Section5 gives a certificate. Its
identities on signed tests and inequalities on one-sided tests are
closed constraints on that compact space: their integrands are
continuous on the compact normal bundle or on the section facets.
Each finite union of lists is handled by one certificate. The
finite-intersection property consequently gives a single certificate
for all lists. This is also why facet body and section allocations
may not be chosen independently in this argument.

Define the weighted cap-boundary measure

    dnu=sum_j lambda_j alpha_j deta,
    W=eta-nu.

Every signed normal-dependent affine physical test yields

    int psi(u) A(z,x) dW=0                           (10)

for arbitrary continuous psi and affine A. Every nonnegative
normal-localized convex potential gives

    int psi(u)Phi(z,x)dW>=0                          (11)

for continuous psi>=0 and continuous convex Phi. The sign follows
because its outward body velocity is -psi Phi, and the polar term
in(8) has nonpositive pairing with that one-sided direction.
Smooth convex tests or finite maxima of affine functions suffice;
uniform approximation on the compact physical range gives the stated
continuous convex class.

Equations(9)--(11) are the general normal-bundle convex-order stress.
They retain arbitrary oblique caps, every coincident-facet branch,
all active compatibility, nonsmooth or flat body boundaries, and
all original measured fibers. On noncoincident body traces alpha_j
is the cap indicator. On a coincident facet it is the consistent
allocation in(6), not an incorrectly imposed closed-cap indicator.

They are necessary for EVERY selected critical circuit cover at a
true local minimum. The certificate can depend on that cover. The
exact simplex example in the separate concave-roof note already
shows why one convenient cover cannot supply the missing numerical
bound by itself.

## 7. Scope

This theorem applies to the unrestricted all-positive attained
finite-base minimum supplied by the earlier counterexample reduction.
It does not require that minimum to be smooth or polytopal, and
does not use the separate fixed-N extremal class. The numerical claim
beta>=Gamma_d/h(P) for arbitrary finite P is now known to be FALSE
by the exact unequal-three-site construction. Consequently neither
these conditions nor their universal-cover quantifier can imply that
claim in full generality. A successful OC argument must retain the
lattice-complete base and its original parity budget; the desired
gamma_d/k(U) implication on that restricted class remains unproved.

The intrinsic lower-dimensional and d=0 cases are not treated by
these boundary-area variations. Those are separate reductions of
the original problem and are not inferred from this necessary
condition on positive d-dimensional fibers.

## 8. A simpler concave defining function gives the same convex order

The essential global convex-potential construction has a shorter
geometric description. On B times R^d define the signed fiber margin

    m(z,x)=min_(|u|=1) [h_z(u)-u.x].                (12)

It is concave: each function inside the minimum is concave in(z,x),
and the hypograph of their infimum is the intersection of their convex
hypographs. Also C={m>=0}. Inside a section, m is the distance to its
boundary; outside, -m is the distance to the section. These distance
identities follow by intersecting the support halfspaces and by the
nearest-point supporting plane, respectively. The concavity statement
itself follows directly from the support formula and requires neither
distance identity.

For a globally convex physical function Phi=A+sum_l t_l Phi_l,
where A is signed affine and t_l>=0, the bodies

    { (z,x):z in B, m(z,x)>=epsilon Phi(z,x) }       (13)

are actual convex variations. They have normal velocity -Phi at every
regular fiber-boundary point, by Section3. The boundedness, positive
fiber interiors, and uniform radial displacement estimates from
Sections2--3 apply verbatim. A common positive continuous homothety
may be composed with (13) to include the signed homothety direction
used for normalization; its first velocity simply adds s u.x.

Run the same finite-test separation and compactness proof with only
these global convex functions, signed affine functions, and the common
homothety. It gives ONE source nu with global physical convex order
nu<=cx eta and the same exact sum lambda=1/beta. Section5 of
`candidate 7278f286325c46c7` then proves
that any physical barycenter-preserving coupling automatically retains
the continuous outer normal, because the fibers are actual sections.
Thus all normal-localized identities and inequalities(10)--(11) follow
afterwards by conditional Jensen.

This is an alternative dependency order, not a new numerical
inequality. It avoids needing the full collection of normal-dependent
potentials to obtain the stated necessary condition. The more general
variations in Section2 remain valid, and prescribed inside-facet
allocations from Section4 remain available in this simpler proof.
